new_statements.rule_in_words: Paite is a tone language (5 tonemes) with no lexical stress contrast; word-level prominence is analysed as a quantity-insensitive syllabic iamb: in compounds/polysyllables the non-final syllables shorten and lose their tone while the final (rightmost) syllable keeps full tone and length, i.e. right-edge (final-syllable) prominence; feet may be binary or unbounded.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; non-head syllables are simply de-toned/shortened.
new_statements.exceptions: Nominalisation with the toned suffix -na: yields left/trochaic prominence on the stem (luak-na:, te:t-na:), attributed to clash avoidance; H-tone spread in reduplicative adverbs gives right-edge prominence. Function words not treated.
new_statements.domain_note: Prosodic word (stem + affixes, compounds) elicited as words and compounds read in isolation by four JNU-student speakers; prominence is diagnosed from tone/vowel-length alternation (Praat F0), not from stress phonetics. Theory-laden (Hayes/Kager metrical terms); the author never states a plain 'stress falls on X' rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Nianglianmoi 2016 describes Paite of Manipur (speakers recorded at JNU; Lamzang treated as standard, Lamka town koine noted); Singh 1985 describes the Lamjang (Lamzang) dialect of Tuithapi village near Churachandpur; Grierson 1904's 'Paite' is the Dapzal variety of the Lushai Hills. All fall under pait1244. Henderson 1965 (wishlist) describes Tedim/Tiddim Chin of Myanmar, a separate glottocode (tedi1235) though authors treat Paite and Tedim as one dialect cluster.

sources.note: Ch.4 'Prosodic Word': Paite feet are quantity-insensitive syllabic iambs; in di-/trisyllabic words non-final syllables shorten/lose tone and only the rightmost syllable projects full tone (right-margin prominence); nominaliser -na gives trochaic (stem) prominence; 'Paite is a weight-insensitive language'; rhythm is controlled by tone alternation. No lexical stress contrast is posited; five tonemes (M, H, L, LH, HL).
